utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You see, I suggest to you, Mr. Treanor - and you've had the advantage of considering all this period and these materials over many years - that it would have been politically absolutely a crude blunder by Mr. Krajisnik, as the Speaker of the Assembly, to associate himself with any such document in this form, given the debate and the toughness of the debate which had been had in the Assembly, in relation to the minority municipalities' proposal, without his having it raised in any way in the Serb Assembly for debate.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see a crude blunder necessarily, and I'm not sure what you mean by "to associate himself with any such documents in this form." You mean that form of document, I suppose. Well, on the face of the document, he's not associated with it. As we know from documents which I offered in my presentation, the SDS as far back as September had adopted a two-track strategy, if I can put it that way, one public, one conspiratorial. This document, I would say, is on the conspiratorial track; therefore, it is not something that people are supposed to be associating themselves with, certainly publicly. The establishment of the Assembly and the decisions of the Assembly were, of course, the public track.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, I put it to you that your approach, and I put it that way, has an air of complete unreality on it. The position was this: There were, in the case presented against Mr. Krajisnik, there were enough copies of this document in the world and they were in enough hands for the possibility of it not becoming widely known within the Serb Assembly to be just about nil, so that the members of the Serb Assembly, if it was a document with official support from the leadership of the SDS, would have come to know that very quickly. And in the light of the debate that there had been on the minority municipalities - I'll put it politely but colloquially - some of the deputies would have been saying -- to appear to have been knocking on his Speaker's office door and they would have been say, "What on earth is going on? We had that -- we had that debate a few weeks ago, whenever it was. You've heard what some of the people have got to say about that. We approved that. You got that through all right. And now you've got some other documents, all this detailed stuff and majority Assembles and you didn't even ask us about it." Isn't that the reality of what would have happened if this document had had the status which you suggest it had?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members of the Bosnian Serb Assembly were almost exclusively members of the SDS. Many of them were members of the Main Board. Many of them - I don't know how many, because we don't know precisely who was at the meeting of the 20th of December - were present at that meeting. The Statutes of the SDS call for acceptance and implementation of party decisions. Dr. Karadzic was very insistent on that. What transpired at that meeting, which would have been the opportunity for -- I'm speculating -- would have been an opportunity for anyone to express their disagreement, they wouldn't have had to go to Mr. Krajisnik to complain. And as I indicated, perhaps the resistance to doing that in certain municipalities is the reason why it may not have been implemented in certain municipalities. When you referred to being associated with a document, I thought you meant in a public manner. As you indicated, there were many copies of the document but, rather interestingly, perhaps it became public -- or got published -- was published in the press only at the beginning of March. So up to that point, they seem to have done a fairly good job in keeping it confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you see there, Mr. Treanor, once again if you -- as often happens, if you don't start from here, you may end up somewhere else. If you give the document the status that you give it and you assume it's what it was and that it had the distribution it had and so on, then introducing the conspiratorial element to explain why it didn't appear publicly in an obvious way is not so difficult. But if the document did not have the status that you describe and if it was a document of the nature with the origin that the Defence is suggesting and if it never was adopted, then you don't need a conspiracy, do you, to explain its lesser prominence? It just wasn't that important a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me address what I think is happening here and then explain briefly why I think it's inappropriate. As I understand it, the witness has repeatedly explained the basis for his conclusions, and there has been ample opportunity to identify, explore, and address those. Now we seem to be engaged in the following exercise in which all of those bases are sort of sequentially eliminated and the witness is asked to speculate about individual pieces of evidence as if the other pieces of evidence did not exist. It can be an interesting philosophical debate, but I don't think it advances our inquiry here. I think it's time-consuming and I think it is resulting in a considerable amount of speculation and effectively argument between counsel and the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It may not matter much from a practical point of view, Your Honour, because I think we probably have explored the issue, this particular issue, as far as we need go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think as a matter of fact that it's quite clear from the point of view of the Defence that if the document would not have had the status as given to it by Mr. Treanor, then of course the way people would have dealt with this document would have been different. Is that the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it is the underlying point. Your Honour, in a -- I don't really want, then, to spend time justifying what I've already done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Which would then take more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you could put a hundred questions in this respect. If the document would not have had the official -- let me just try to invent one question. If some bunch of unorganised people would have produced a document in which a certain role is given to the president of the -- to give secret instructions, well, you could expect that someone would ever go to that president and say, "Do you know that your name is abused for that?" You could put thousands and thousands of questions starting from a different point of view, but it's quite clear to me, and I think to the Bench, that if the document had a different status, that you would expect other things to happen related to that document. Yes. Then if you say that -- if that's the most important thing, I would like to invite you to move on to your next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'm more than happy to, Your Honour, because I think really that point had -- well, it's a matter of argument whether it has emerged clearly. Apparently it hasn't emerged clearly. But it was necessary for me also just to explore how far certain elements of Mr. Treanor's conclusions depend upon the reliability of other elements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And we've done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The point was clear already quite some time ago. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I invite you to consider this possibility, Mr. Treanor, that the -- and it is -- I put it forward just as a possibility for you to consider, that discussion on the 19th of December could, consistently with a great deal of the material we've seen, have revolved around the recommendation in the Assembly in relation to -- adopted by the Serb Assembly in relation to what I call minority municipalities, rather than discussion about the Variant A and B document.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed the discussion would have involved a lot of things. I don't know what the discussion was, unfortunately. Indeed maybe there wasn't any discussion of the A and B document. Maybe it was simply distributed or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, and you don't yourself know and can't tell, is that correct, whether any dissemination of the Variant A and B document around that time was official or unofficial?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we said in the report that it seems likely on the evidence that it was - I don't know -- remember the word that we used - distributed, issued at that meeting. Wherever it was issued, it must have been official, in my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has this not been dealt with now four or five times, on the officiality of the document and distribution. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just go back to the very first page of the Variant A and B document and the reference in the top left-hand corner of I think every version, "Serbian Democratic Party, Bosnia and Herzegovina Main Board" or "Main Committee," depending which translation one chooses. Is it a possibility that this document, that is intended to mean that the document was addressed to the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I take that to be the origin of the document. That's usually where the letterhead, if you will, is located, indicating the origin of a letter, so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That would be the -- and that would be the -- the custom or practice in Bosnia and Herzegovina to --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm just referring from memory to the various letters of Dr. Karadzic, for instance. And if it was being addressed to somebody, I would expect to see it in -- not in the nominative case, which is here, but in the dative case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm going to move on, Your Honours, to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I want to consider now the issue of the expanded Presidency, Mr. Treanor. Just to remind ourselves, Mr. Krajisnik is alleged to have been a member of a five-person expanded Presidency from the 2nd of June to the 17th of December, 1992. You cover some aspects of this matter in your report at paragraph 260 and following, and you very helpfully set out some of the relevant constitutional provisions. I'll take them from there, because it's far easier for us to do it that way. You dealt with this in your evidence in chief. "To summarise, on the 12th of May" -- and this is paragraph 260 of your report -- "on the 12th of May the Bosnian Serb Assembly passed a law amending and supplementing the constitutional law, and that provided that until the president of the republic was elected there should be a three-member Presidency elected by the Assembly of the Serb People," and Dr. Karadzic, Dr. Plavsic, and Mr. Koljevic were elected on that day. On the 1st or 2nd of June - and this is really the key point so far as Mr. Krajisnik's involvement is concerned, and key point in the case put against him - is that the Presidency then adopted - and we look at 261, paragraph 261 of your report - adopted the law on supplementing the constitutional law for implementing the Constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and added paragraph 3 to Article 5, and that's a key paragraph because it provides - and you cite it in your report - "During a state of war, the Presidency shall be expanded to include the president of the National Assembly" - of course, that was Mr. Krajisnik; that's where he comes in - "and the president of the Government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And we know - and there's no dispute about this - that no state of war was formally declared in 1992; that instead, if you like, on the 15th of April there was a declaration of an imminent threat of war, which was a different thing. So so far we're in agreement about these basics, are we, Mr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. An imminent threat of war was declared on April the 15th. And I am not aware of any similar declaration of a state of war. In fact, there is some discussion later on in the year of the fact that in fact there was no such thing, but then we have on the 17th of December a declaration, if you will, on the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. And so the two stages or the two dates which are material, then, for this particular point, then, following the 1st of June - and you very clearly and helpfully record this at 264 of your report - that on the 30th of November a meeting of what was described as the Presidency discussed the legal position, and in particular the fact that in that provision of the Constitution that we referred to a few moments ago, which had been added on the 12th of May, it was only a state of war which triggered off what is referred to now as the expanded Presidency, the five-person Presidency. This was dealt with, wasn't it, by -- when considered by that meeting, described as a meeting of the Presidency on the 30th of November. It was dealt with effectively by shelving the issue for the time being. But that shelving came to an end on the 17th of December, when the declaration of an end of -- the end of the war took place, as you describe, and so constitutionally everything went back to square one as far as the Presidency was concerned, the original constitutional provisions.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the 17th of December, another reform of the Presidency was carried out. The offices of two vice-presidents were created, which had not existed in the original Constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Treanor, if I may interrupt. I don't think there's any disagreement between us. I think I had cited accurately as far as I went from your report. Your report says in paragraph 265: "The Assembly restructured the Presidency by reverting to the original constitutional provision for one president." And then you do say: "But also passing a package of amendments which created a dual vice-president."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So we're at one on that. And amendments of the vice-president. But at the level of Presidency, as you accurately and very succinctly set out there, just went back to the original constitutional provision of a single president.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. And that issue, which -- would you agree that issue that had been shelved on the 30th of November, about whether the amend the Constitution, to introduce a reference to imminent threat of war; that actually was superseded, then, by the decision on the 17th of December?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, which appears to embody the results of whatever deliberations may have taken place after the 30th of November as to how to handle the situation. Another action that was taken about this time was the creation of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, it -- Mr. Treanor, you might wish to answer this by saying that we have for you as a non-lawyer reached the limits or are going beyond the limits of your legal expertise, but --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, I think as a political matter, I think they addressed this issue, which was a problem. And I would say that three things were done: They created the Supreme Command; they made some more changes in the Presidency, going back to one president and then creating two vice-presidents on the 17th of December; and they declared an end to the war. This seems to be a package of measures to address those concerns and other issues at that time, but they seem to be interrelated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Treanor, when I indicated you might wish to answer this by saying that for you as a lawyer we might have reached the limits or we're going beyond the limits of your legal expertise, I was actually referring to the question I was about to ask you. The question I was about to ask you or what I was going to put to you was this: That there was a clear defect, wasn't there, in the sense that the conditions triggering off the five-person expanded Presidency -- or the condition - namely, a state of war - had not arisen.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's one of the defects in that particular document and the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's certainly one of them. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in any sense, it's enough on this own, Mr. Treanor, this defect. I'm not going to explore any other defects at the moment. So we're agreed there was that defect, that the condition for triggering off that expanded Presidency had not arisen. Secondly, it was never -- well, in the end, after the shelving on the 30th of November and then the decisions on the 17th of December, that defect was never technically cured and in the end in fact no attempt was made to cure it, because there was no purported retrospective amendment and, in fact, no amendment to cure that defect, was there?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you mean by during the defect adopting something of the nature that -- the nature of what was discussed in the Presidency on the 30th of November, certainly that was never done. And, on the other hand, a state of war was never declared, as we mentioned earlier. So that wasn't done either. So this problem was not tackled head-on in that fashion, thirdly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So why I referred to the possible limits, as far as legal issues are concerned, Mr. Treanor, is this: That -- I just put it to you that from a strictly legal, technical point of view there never had validly been under the Constitution a five-person expanded Presidency and nothing was ever done to ratify the -- or to cure by ratification or some other way that invalidity.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you certainly have reached the limit of my legal expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's a perfectly fair answer, Mr. Treanor. The -- and then so far as -- so if we, then, move away for the moment - and when I say "for the moment," I think for the rest of your evidence, Mr. Treanor, or the rest of your cross-examination from that legal position - in a nutshell, because a great deal of this ground has been covered, what the -- and if I call it "the expanded Presidency," now, it's with that caveat. So I'm talking about the position between the beginning of June and 17th of December. What that group, the minutes of whose meetings we apparently have, actually did, so far as you're concerned, you only know what you see on those documents and any other documents that you have access to in connection with your report.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. The only thing I know about the activities of the Presidency are based on the documents that I've seen, which are not only the minutes. There are some -- we have some of the decisions that they issued, alluded to -- I used a couple of those in my presentation, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I think I referred slightly more widely to available documentation.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, for example, whether a particular person was or wasn't present at a particular meeting, you -- if you see a person listed as present at a particular meeting, you have no basis on which to do anything other than make the normal common sense starting point assumption that the person was there.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So if I say, for example, that there is the Twenty-sixth Session of the Presidency which was dated 23rd August 1992, so that's right within that period of the expanded Presidency, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't think we need the actual document at the moment. It's a very simple point. Mr. Krajisnik is shown as present. He was not in fact present that day. The reason he was not present was an unhappy one; that was actually the day that his wife died and he was in Belgrade on that day. And he was not present for that reason at the -- at that Twenty-sixth Session. But that's just an example. You would of course have -- this is correct? You would have no knowledge whatsoever. You would have no way of knowing whether Mr. Krajisnik was correctly or incorrectly shown as present at that meeting or indeed any other meeting.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I then ask you about the National Security Council. The National Security Council was created - and you've covered this helpfully in your evidence - was created by the Serb Assembly at its session of the 27th of March, 1992, and it was the decision that appears at file 11, tab 116. I don't think -- because we've seen lots of these pieces of paper before I don't think I need to trouble you or the Tribunal to keep delving into the files again. Again, it was set up as advisory organ of the Assembly, wasn't it? That's ground that we've already covered. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it does. And it was responsible for its work to the Assembly. That was the formal position in the establishment of the National Security Council.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're reading it to me now. I don't have it before me, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, well, take my word for it, please, Mr. Treanor. It's absolutely ready checkable by anybody in a moment. And the president of the republic was the ex officio chairman. You recall that.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then you say in your report at -- this is at paragraph 258. You say that the -- in reality the SNB, which is the same thing -- the National Security Council -- the SNB became the central Bosnian Serb Crisis Staff with a composition mirroring that of the regional and local Crisis Staffs which form, you say, the subject of a separate report, and that while it was supposed to be an advisory body - as in the technical provisions I just cited to you - concerning itself with interests of the Serbian People, it acted as a de facto expanded presidency and exercised the powers of the Presidency. May we look, then, at bundle 12, file 12, please, at tab 127. If we go to, well, page 1, in the first place. I did give the tab number, I think, did I? 127.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the session of the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, we're back to the good old 12th of May session --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- of the Serb Assembly: Item 3, Confirmation of the decisions and other legislation adopted by the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." And then -- that's the agenda. And then over the page, page 2, we get that item as the decision. "The Assembly unanimously confirmed the following decisions adopted by the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," and then a number. I won't read through them, because they can be read. But just to mention, for example, number 7, "Decision on proclaiming imminent threat of war"; not an unimportant one. And then 8 was "Decision of the establishment of penal and correctional organisations in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." We don't see, do we, any equivalent adoption by the Assembly of National Security Council decisions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The decisions of the National Security Council, in so far as they needed to be embodied in publicly issued decisions such as the decision on proclaiming the imminent threat of war or the decision on the establishment of penal and correctional organisations, both of which were published in the Official Gazette after they had -- after this verification took place, those documents were issued in the name of and presumably signed by the two acting presidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So what had happened was that the National -- in that situation, then, the National Security Council, having been set up as an advisory board only and having the obligation to report to the Assembly, what you're saying is that in practice, then, the route for getting decisions -- well, the formal route for decisions to be taken and implemented in that situation was that it was done by the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If we go to -- back to bundle -- no, to bundle 11 it will be, please, tab 118. We've seen this letter before. This is a letter dated 4th of April, 1992 from Dr. Karadzic addressed to the Serb Assembly. And he was, as I think you've already pointed out, he was not technically the right person to be the president of the National Security Council under Article 3 of the -- of its, well, constitution, if I might call it that, because it was the president of the republic, wasn't it, who was ex officio to be the president of the National Security Council?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would point out in this connection that the copy of the decision we have is not a signed and dated copy, and it was not published in the Official Gazette for I think a rather interesting technical reason, but it would appear from the record of the Assembly session that that was the text that was adopted. So if we take that as our premise, then yes, he should not have been the president of this body.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is this rather interesting technical reason a relevant technical reason, Mr. Treanor, or just interesting? Because if it's just interesting, then we'll have to suppress our curiosity.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would appear to me that it was not published not for any desire to keep it secret perhaps but there was a problem that arose connected with the move of the SDS leaders from downtown Sarajevo to Pale, which took place very soon after the March sessions. And I'm getting this from what was told to me in Pale by the individuals involved with the production of the Official Gazette, that the materials that had been prepared for publication in the next issue of the Official Gazette were lost during that period; and therefore, once they got to Pale, they had to reconstruct a number of things, and you'll find some peculiarities in the Official Gazette in that connection. Namely, you'll find documents signed by Dr. Karadzic as president of the Presidency or something on dates before he occupied that position. And there's a large gap in the pagination in the Official Gazette for that reason, apparently. And this was apparently among the items that was totally lost, and therefore never published in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it's correct, isn't it, there's no record this letter of Dr. Karadzic's of the 4th of April, there's no record of any National Security Council decision in terms of that letter?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's the only record we have -- the only record I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And at the time, as I think you pointed out, Mr. Karadzic -- Dr. Karadzic had no executive position, apart from the fact he was president of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You referred to a transcript - and it's in the -- not surprisingly, it's in the bundle of transcripts - it's tab, or section 28 of the transcript of speeches binder. I'm sorry, my terminology is slipping. The intercepts -- the intercepts bundle, I think we call it. It's got transcripts of intercepts and speeches. P67, anyway -- 66 in English -- it is 67. And you in your -- you dealt with this matter in your evidence in chief. It's at page 686 of the transcript. And then what you said was -- I'll just get that, if I may. Oh, it's come over in the transcript today as 686. The page number is 1686, 1686. And you referred to the conversation that we have in the intercepts bundle at 28, the conversation between Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Krajisnik. And then you -- which is very short, and it says the person appointed -- Mr. Krajisnik says, when they finally get on the telephone together, [As read] "Hey, Nikola." And Mr. Koljevic says, "What's up, Momo?" Mr. Krajisnik, "Are you coming to my place tonight?" Mr. Koljevic, "tonight at 7.00, right. Yes. Radovan told me and I'll be there. All right. He knows full we'll can you tell discuss that at my place. Deal. All right. See you there. All right. Bye." So that's pretty short and sweet. You said in your evidence that this would in effect have been a meeting of the National Security Council. "We certainly at least have three of its most prominent members mentioned in this conversation. Who else was going to be at that meeting precisely, I don't know." Do you -- your conclusion that that would in effect have been a meeting of the National Security Council, are you also using the existence of Dr. Karadzic's letter to support that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I was trying to link them. First of all, let me address a matter connected to this particular conversation and another conversation that took place on the same day between, I believe it was Dr. Karadzic and Dr. Koljevic, which is also dated the 4th of April. I believe that the date of these conversations is incorrect now having -- I was looking into a related matter, that is, the matter of mobilisation by the Presidency of SRBiH which figured in the April 4th letter of Dr. Karadzic. Having reviewed some documents in that connection just recently, it appears that the sequence of events is as follows: There was a meeting of the Presidency of Bosnia, of BH. On the afternoon of the 3rd of April -- Dr. Koljevic and Dr. Plavsic were both present at that meeting, according to the minutes. And a decision was made that individual municipalities could mobilise their Territorial Defence organisations if they thought the situation warranted. There was also some discussion at that meeting about Dr. Plavsic going to Bijeljina and Dr. Koljevic going to Banja Luka the next day, I believe, the 4th. Now, there was another meeting on the 4th. Dr. Koljevic and Dr. Plavsic were not present at that meeting, because they were in the cities I indicated. At that session -- and it was a very extended session. The minutes indicate that it lasted for a period of days. I don't know precisely what the circumstances was, whether they were all there at all time, but obviously it was a -- a crisis situation. At that meeting another decision regarding mobilisation was taken, basically that, well, everyone should mobilise in fact. That decision was taken without the participation of the Bosnian Serb members, because they were not there. Dr. Karadzic's letter was issued on the 4th and appears to be a response to the decision taken on the 3rd, that is, the partial mobilisation, if I can put it that way. Therefore, I believe that these conversations took place on the 3rd of April. In the conversation with Dr. Karadzic, Dr. Koljevic indicates that he had been at a presidency meeting that day. So I think these conversations took place on the 3rd of April and the meeting in the evening was on the evening of the 3rd of April. And the letter was, of course, issued on the 4th of April and was in fact published in the press on the 5th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether you're the right person to be able to answer this, Mr. Treanor, but then the question is, then, where did the date of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the 4th of April for this transcript come from?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the date on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the question was where that comes from on the transcript, if you at the same time, if your testimony is that more likely this conversation would have taken place on the 3rd. So I think Mr. Stewart is trying to get an answer on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I guess my answer to how did it get on the transcript, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that's fair enough. I thought perhaps you're not the right person to answer that. Of course, there's an alternative possibility, which is that the date that we have been given all along for this transcript is the correct date, that it did take place on the 4th of April and that it is not -- the conversation is not referring to a meeting being set up from which this letter emerged.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is certainly possible that there's no connection between the meeting and the letter. I think I linked them in my testimony as a sequence of events that was taking place. It was, rather, my supposition that a response to the mobilisation decision that was taken on the 3rd would have been discussed most likely - I won't say inevitably; that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It looks, doesn't it, Mr. Treanor, as if a perfectly reasonable possibility, given that these people know each other and given the brevity of the conversation between Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Krajisnik, is that they did arrange to meet in the evening of the 4th of April and actually that meeting simply doesn't have anything to do with that particular letter.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, to my knowledge, at this point Dr. Koljevic was in Banja Luka on the 4th of April. He had attended a meeting of the Presidency on the 3rd of April, which was referred to in his conversation with Dr. Karadzic and that conversation also referred to having a meeting that night. This particular conversation is one in, well, a series of at least two interrelated conversations about holding a meeting on that particular evening, and one of them is certainly connected with the meeting of the Presidency that Dr. Koljevic had attended on that day. So I at this point infer that this conversation took place on the 3rd of April and that there were plans to have a meeting at 1900 hours on the evening of the 3rd of April. Whether that meeting in fact ever took place, of course I don't know. The only -- the next thing that we do know is that we have the letter of Mr. Karadzic dated the 4th of April. And as I say, that letter was published in the press on the 5th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, we don't know whether the meeting took place. We don't know whether the letter was discussed at the meeting, do we?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not definitely, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stewart. I see that you're looking at the clock; so did I. Before adjourning --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May I just mention the book. We produced the -- as Your Honour directed, we produced the pages either side. We haven't found out that there is a published English translation of the book. In the usual way we can't prove a negative, we haven't established there isn't. But at the moment ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I -- first of all, as far as the environment is concerned, is it right? Yes, this is 101 and 103, where already we received 102. So this is the environment. If no English translation does exist, I would invite the Prosecution to read the context and to see whether you could agree on whether we need any further translation apart from the part translated in court. Yes? I also understood, Mr. Tieger, that you had copied the many, many documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct. Your Honour, we can distribute them now or during the break. As you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are we going to further deal with it? I don't think so. So, therefore, I think distribution during the break would be fine. Then I have another smaller issue, Mr. Stewart. Yesterday you confronted the witness with a different distance between the offices of Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic, which in view of the testimony given until that moment was, well, at least indicated that what the witness had said was not a bit wrong but entirely wrong. As far as distance is concerned -- and then you said, "Well, there might be an issue of time. And I'll further --" I'd like to have this either clarified or you the three kilometres are not to be -- could be ignored.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm proposing to clear it up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then we'll hear from you after the next break. We'll have a break until ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, I'm not quite sure which bundle you've got. Have you got number 12 at the moment or number 11 or which? Oh, you've got the intercepts. I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could we have 11, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And if we'd go to tab 120. You referred to this in your evidence. The transcript reference is -- evidence in chief -- is at 1690 as "the first record we have of a session of the National Security Council proper." But in fact, of course, it was a joint meeting of the National Security Council and the government, wasn't it, as we see?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the position was that the Security the National Security Council - I think we've covered this ground - actually had technically no formal powers at all, did it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of that -- the text of the decision we've seen, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So that where we have a joint meeting of the National Security Council and the government, the Serbian Republic, that any powers of, if you like, that joint meeting are going to be the normal executive powers of the government.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe that, as indicated by the decisions published in the Gazette which were signed by the Presidency -- or by the acting presidents and later verified by the Assembly, that decisions were made which were within the purview of the Assembly but taken by the Presidency under its emergency powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We may be slightly at cross-purposes here, Mr. Treanor. If there was a -- at a joint meeting of the National Security Council and the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the National Security Council itself technically having no executive powers, the government having the usual executive powers of a government, the government's powers were all that that joint meeting had.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least one member of -- one of the acting Presidencies was present at this meeting. And as a result of this very meeting, a decision on the imminent threat of war is issued, which is discussed in these minutes, signed by the two acting presidents. If -- certainly, if both of them had been present, then it would have been within -- apparently within their prerogative, barring any legal niceties which I cannot address, to take decisions in their own name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, there is no issue between us on that. If all the members of a particular organ are present and make the decision, then it is normally going to be difficult to quarrel with that. All right. Well, I won't pursue that point any more. At the end of this minute that we're looking at at tab 120, we see again council president Dr. Karadzic signing. Would you agree that the key point here seems to be that Dr. Karadzic, having assumed the position as president of the National Security Council - although apparently inconsistent with the technical requirement that it should be ex officio the president of the republic - in practice he's taking the leadership of the government here.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: By "government" do you mean the -- what could also be called the Council of Ministers?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- that would do just as well for my purposes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is a prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, this is rather what I'm suggesting to you, Mr. Treanor, that where you have a government and a prime minister - I think he's called the president of the government often, isn't he, in the documentation that we see --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Where you have a government, and I'll use the terminology prime minister, because it is simpler in the context, and then you have another body here, the National Security Council and Dr. Karadzic is the chairman or the president of that body, and they are meeting together, those two bodies, and then it turns out that it's not the prime minister who chairs and signs the minute and takes charge but it is Dr. Karadzic. It's pretty clear, isn't it, that whatever the formal position, if you like, the prime minister has had to move over and his seat effectively is being taken by Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I see what you're driving at and we're getting into areas of legal interpretation. But when we wrote the report and indeed now my conception is that during this period the acting presidents were -- had assumed emergency powers under the Constitution and issued decisions on the basis of those emergency powers. I believe it's Article 81 which gave the presidents of the republic, or in this case the acting presidents the authority to make decisions which would ordinarily be within the purview of the Assembly. Now, among the things that were within the purview of the Assembly were issues related to the government. The government, of course, reports to the Assembly. It's appointed by the Assembly, can be relieved by the Assembly, must answer questions from the Assembly, et cetera. Therefore during this emergency period, that function -- the functions of the Assembly are exercised by the president of the republic, so the president of the republic in effect becomes the Assembly. So it's not a question of the prime minister having to move over for anybody. The prime minister is always subordinate to the Assembly, always answers to the Assembly, and simply during these emergency periods that position is taken by the support of the republic, or in the case the acting presidents. So I don't see that the prime minister has had to move over. If anyone moved over, it was the two acting presidents, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At tab 123 of this same bundle we see a document which is apparently signed -- we don't see the actual signature, but by the president of the government of the prime minister, Dr. Ranko Bjelic [phoen]. And it's an excerpt from the "Instructions for the Operation of Crisis Headquarters of the Serb People in the Municipalities." And I just wonder if you can confirm that in the original Serbian that the word or words which are represented in English by "Crisis Headquarters" are the same as the words used at the foot of the Variants A and B document.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "of the foot of the document."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, at the very end of the Variant A and B, where it's signed, in effect.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah yes. Yes. As far as I can recollect, what that says is "Crisis Staff of the SDS." This refers to "Crisis Staffs," in the plural, "of the Serbian People."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I beg your pardon. So apart from the pluralising, but the word for "Crisis Staff" or "Crisis Staffs" --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the same term.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- would be from the same?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the same term, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are one or two relatively minor points, including the question that Your Honour raised before the adjournment about the location of offices and so on to clear up in a moment with Mr. Treanor. I simply wanted to make clear, having done what I've done by way of cross-examination of Mr. Treanor over the last few days, what I'm not going to do and why I'm not going to do it. I am not going to put to Mr. Treanor what we see that he can't actually himself give evidence about, which was beyond this documentation what was actually happening, because after all, Mr. Treanor wasn't there. He's not a factual witness in relation to that. He's very frankly indicated that knowing what he knows and having studied the history of politics, he's working from the documents, he's here to explain the documents, he's here to put them into context. So, Your Honour, we conceive it would be a rather futile and wasteful exercise to be batting backwards and forwards to Mr. Treanor factual propositions of which he can't say anything at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just check. I take it that you take it, Mr. Treanor, that you agree with the characterisation of your specific knowledge or expertise. I wouldn't say you have no knowledge at all. Perhaps it's not first-hand knowledge. It's not the most reliable source on what happened on the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would not like to speak to anything that is not encompassed within the documents with which I am familiar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's understood. And I think it's fair to do it this way. This, of course, could cause at -- this might not be a major problem for this expert witness, that if we hear evidence on what happened on the ground and if this raises all kinds of questions in relation to documents, that it might be that we need Mr. Treanor again to further elaborate on the documents. Is that -- I take it, Mr. Tieger, that that's a possibility you also envisage if we do it the way as suggested by Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, the question of the location, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll put the position to you and then -- as we have it and then you can simply indicate whether you agree or not, please. Mr. Krajisnik worked -- while in Sarajevo, Mr. Krajisnik worked at all times in and from the Assembly building which was on the other side of the road from the Holiday Inn. But from late March 1992, Mr. Karadzic had a suite at the Holiday Inn and he used that suite for meetings and to talk to people. It was used as some sort of an office; some sort of a working environment as well. But also, at some 3 kilometres - and that is the distance I gave it, it remains the distance - at some 3 kilometres from the Assembly building where Mr. Krajisnik had his office was the old Assembly building and old goes back, of course, to the communist regime, which had actually come to be known as the Deputies' Club. That was the description of it. And that was a building where the SDS at period, 1991 and 1992, until, of course, everything moved to Pale eventually, but had three offices and those remained as the SDS offices as long as their operations were in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to confess, having just said about speaking from the documents that my knowledge of this area is rather tangential. I was under the impression the SDS offices had moved to the Holiday Inn sometime in the autumn of 1991, but I -- that's just an impression that I have. I don't know what the evidence is. But I can seek to clarify that point if necessary. I'm not sure what the significance of this is, other than a simple one of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, doubt whether we --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: So what you're saying may be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, I doubt whether we will need to trouble you again on this particular matter. I just wanted to make it clear. I think what I put to you earlier about this was incomplete, perhaps than actually wrong. But I wanted to clear it and make it plain what we were saying was the physical layout.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that completes the questions. We would tender into evidence, if it is the appropriate moment, the letters that were referred to by Mr. Treanor, and then I had identified those letters. That's the letter of the 30th of July -- copies I've got, of course -- the 30th of July, 2001 from Mr. Blewitt to the liaison officer in Republika Srpska and the reply, the date 5th of November, 2001. We have both those letters in B/C/S and in English in a clip together. I -- does that -- they're clipped together at the moment. Does that mean they should be disentangled and made 1 and 2, the English and the B/C/S versions? It's a very small clip of papers, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think for reasons of consistency, it would be better to, because that's the structure we always have is the .1 being the translation of the original. But now, of course, we have here the problem that the original sent by Mr. Blewitt may have been in English and the original received may have been the B/C/S version. Therefore, perhaps -- but I'm also looking at you, Madam Registrar -- I think we could deal with them as a bundle of --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's very helpful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of correspondence in the original and translation, letters of the 30th of July and 5th of November, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I think Ms. Cmeric had intelligently anticipated Your Honours' view of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We highly appreciate that, Ms. Cmeric.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be Defence Exhibit Number D9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any need to re-examine the witness, Mr. Tieger? And perhaps but I first should consult my colleagues and see whether we would have any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi would have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Witness, I should like to ask you a few very brief questions. I need some clarification. First of all, I refer to what you wrote in your report on page 40. The title is "Deputies' Club." Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You wrote the following: "[In English] "Karadzic once --" [Interpretation] No, I'm sorry. [In English] [Previous translation continues] "... was of course a member of the Deputies' Club and its doyen." Then, further, you said that "Mr. Maksimovic was the chairman of the Deputies' Club."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So my question in relation to that is: What exactly do you mean by "doyen"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a reference to the fact that Mr. Krajisnik would have been the senior deputy in the club from the point of view of the position that he occupied in the Assembly. Various deputies in the Assembly including deputies of the SDS were elected to be chairman and vice chairman of various commissions, presidents of the individual or vice-presidents of the individual chambers. So there were various offices within the Assembly as a body, and he occupied the highest office in the Assembly. So that is what is being referred to there, as opposed to Mr. Maksimovic, who within the structure of the Assembly did not occupy as high as position as Mr. Krajisnik but was the president of the Deputies' Club. Which is not to say that ordinarily the president of the Deputies' Club would have been the Speaker or the president of the Assembly. But that's the reference to the fact that Mr. Krajisnik was the senior official who was a member in that club.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's precisely my question. Because you say, and rightly so, that Mr. Krajisnik was the president of the Assembly, and in a certain sense he was the doyen of the deputies. However, within the Deputies' Club it was not him who was elected president but someone else. So I don't see which role is played by the president of the Deputies' Club, despite the fact that -- that is, I have an impression that the club did indeed play a rather important role.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The role of the president of the Deputies' Club I believe is the -- your concern here. Each party represented in the Assembly had a Deputies' Club. The clubs were recognised within the rules of procedure of the Assembly. They were allocated offices, that type of thing, to have meetings, at which they would determine the position of their party group within the Assembly - the club is the name they called them - when it came to particular legislative issues. How are we going to vote on this issue? So they would have meetings and have discussions. The person chairing those sessions, and we do have records of some of those sessions, is the president of club. So we see Dr. -- or Mr. Maksimovic chairing meetings of the Deputies' Club and being the president of the club and having to chair those sessions undoubtedly entailed quite a bit of extra work for Mr. Maksimovic, aside from his other duties as a deputy. And I'm not sure whether he was also a member or a chairman of any of the Assembly commissions or committees. But presumably it was an amount of work that the club, and perhaps Mr. Krajisnik, felt that could not easily be combined with Mr. Krajisnik's duties as president of the Assembly, which also undoubtedly took up quite a bit of time. So I think that it was probably not unusual that whichever Deputies' Club the presidents of the Assembly was a member of - and let's remember that this was the first multiparty assembly in BH - would not have been a part of the club because there would have been too much work involved in occupying the two positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do I understand correctly that Mr. Krajisnik did not play a role which would have been important within the Deputies' Club?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he certainly participated in discussions in the Deputies' Club. And the only thing that we know the Deputies' Club really did, based on the documents we have, is have meetings and discuss their position on various issues. And it was certainly open to Mr. Krajisnik to participant in those discussions, and I believe he did, as reflected in documents which have been used in the course of my presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let me move on to another question which has to do with what you say in your report on page 48, line 2, and I quote: "[In English] It is likely that some informal group or body within the top SDS leadership had determined," and so on. [Interpretation] So my question in relation to that is as follows: When you composed your report, did you want to say that his instructions were formulated at the Presidency of the SDS, at the Presidency of the party, be it via a formal organ or an informal body? Or does that open up a possibility that it was a completely different body, an informal body, which was not necessarily integrated into what you termed as "the leadership of the SDS"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the SDS had a single president. There was no collective Presidency. There was one president; that was Dr. Karadzic. Did he write the document? I don't know. But it would certainly appear that he knew of the existence of the document and its contents at the latest by the 18th or 19th of December, those being the dates of the telephone conversations, if the dates are correct, with Mr. Djogo and Mr. Novakovic that I referred to, in which he makes reference to -- appears to make reference to the contents of the document. So he was apparently aware of the preparation of the document and aware of the fact that it was going to be distributed -- well, that -- that on the 20th - I think it's fair to say on the basis of those conversations - that that document would be distributed and that that was a very important meeting that he had to attend. Mr. Djogo had wanted him to go elsewhere on that day, but he had so say, no, that I'm going to an important meeting. So it appears that Dr. Karadzic was privy to that document by that point. Again, whether he drafted it, whether he asked someone else to draft it, we just don't know. The only thing that we do know is we cannot find any trace of the discussion and adoption of that document within the minutes or records of such meetings of formal SDS organs as we have. It appears to me quite likely that Dr. Karadzic asked some group of, as is put here, informal group of probably what he regarded as experts to draft the document for him in order to meet certain contingencies which he foresaw may arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but my question is more simple than that. I wonder what your intention was when you wrote the following sentence: "[In English] [Previous translation continues] ... Group or body within the top SDS leadership." [Interpretation] Because you explained already to us what your point of view was when it comes to the term "leadership." You also quoted -- you identified a number of individuals whom you thought belonged to the leadership group. When you wrote your report, what did you have in mind? Did you have in mind those same individuals who are identified in your report at several places as being the formal leadership of a party?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I see your point now, Your Honour. I believe that when we wrote that we had in mind some group of individuals from among those whom we knew that Dr. Karadzic was accustomed to consulting; that is, members of the Main Board or the Executive Board or maybe even the party council, some group composed of individuals from those party organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. And my last question is actually a clarification. On several occasions you referred to the aspect of conspiracy of the party, and you mentioned the fact that there were two systems within the party, one that was declared public and the other one which was secret, so to speak. Did you base your conclusions on the fact that -- on the sole fact that some of the individuals were given codes, name codes, in order not to reveal their identity during their conversations? Was it only on the basis of that fact that you drew the conclusion that the party actually had and applied a method of conspiracy, so to speak? Because if I understand correctly your testimony - and let me perhaps clarify my question - the policy and the objective of -- the objectives of the party were publicly declared, and I don't see there any aspect of conspiracy, apart from the fact that it was at one point decided that certain individuals would be given code names, which turned out to be useful because their conversations were intercepted.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the idea of the two tracks emerges from the documents from early September 1991, which I used in my presentation, which uses precisely that type of language, that the party should act on two tracks, one public and one conspiratorial. By its nature, conspiratorial activity is secret and seeks not to leave behind any traces, certainly any documentary traces. I linked the code issue with that as one possible manifestation of that type of activity, and I think in the course of our discussion today, if not earlier, I have linked the Variant A and B document with that type of activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. [In English] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, I also have a question to you. I'll read to you the last line of the letter that has just been tendered into evidence under number D9. It reads: "The Main Board, as well as any other SDS body never considered or instructed the organisation and activation of Serb people in Bosnia and Herzegovina at its sessions. We were informed that such instructions were given by a certain number of retired officers of the former Yugoslav People's Army." Is there any documentary evidence that any SDS body, either during sessions, which I understand to be formal sessions, or outside of such sessions, ever considered the organisation - I'm not yet talking about the activation - the organisation of Serb people in Bosnia and Herzegovina? What I'm seeking is this is a, I would say, very broad denial that goes, I would say, far beyond the Variant A and B document, and I ask you to tell us whether in the documents you've studied you find anything that would be inconsistent with this very broad denial of the Main Board or any other SDS body never considered or instructed the organisation and activation of Serb people.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that is quite broad. I think that I have presented documents in the course of my testimony which would indicate that various SDS organs considered issues which could be considered -- which could be classified under that heading. For instance, the establishment of the Assembly of the Serbian People was considered at party meetings prior to the establishment of that Assembly. We've also seen documents related to a Main Board meeting, an Executive Board meeting in, I believe, late November, at which they considered various issues which they recommended to the Assembly for adoption which could be classified under that heading. I would also remark that -- or remind the Court that as far as I'm aware, the SDS lost its pre-April 1992 archive when they evacuated Sarajevo. We have many documents from that archive which we referred to, as I mentioned yesterday, as Cabinet B of the Sarajevo collection. Whether that represents the entire archive as it may have existed at one point in time, I don't know, but the point is that it is not now available to the SDS, so that they would be in a rather poor position to respond to that type of inquiry, except perhaps by consulting surviving members of those bodies and asking them whether any -- what types of matters were considered. But they would not have an archive to consult to determine what they did during that period, because basically we have the archive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My next question is that the letter says that "We were informed that such instructions were given by retired officers of the JNA." Did you ever ask for the source of this information?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that we did, Your Honour. We may have, but I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any other source that would support the retired officers of the former Yugoslav People's Army as, I would say, the driving force behind giving instructions? I'm not saying whether there were any army officers involved, but here it's mainly put on the plate of the army's officers rather than anyone else. Is there any support for the existence of such a group or for these army or retired officers to be the driving force behind this activity or perhaps other activities?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that there is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then finally, you have made no reference to this letter in your report, did you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This report -- this letter at least gives, well, let me say, a different version of what happened and where you specifically dealt with the question of who distributed any instructions, could you tell us why you did not, if it were only in a footnote, to give us this different version of who's responsible for the adoption perhaps and distribution of these A and B -- the Variant A and B document; although it doesn't say specifically that, but that's the tendency, I would say, of this answer.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's an interesting question, Your Honour. I'm not sure whether we even considered that. We may have. But if we did, and the same -- and we didn't use it, it's the same reason why we didn't consider it. We were writing our report on the basis of contemporaneous documentation, that is, documents produced during the period of the conflicts and primarily documents produced at the time of the events, that is, the records of the Assembly session that had just taken place, that sort of thing. Using a document that was produced far after the end of the conflicts is not something that I would ordinarily even think of doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although it is directly related to contemporaneous documents, contemporaneous to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it -- well, yes, I mean, it relates to this document. That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because sometimes if there's unclarity -- if something is unclear, you point at that and say this is not entirely clear, that's not entirely clear. Would the existence of this letter not have urged you to adopt one or two lines saying, "Well, although a different explanation has been given --" because you make inferences. There's no signature. There's a relatively unknown group of people or organ or whatever you'd call it which raises some questions, and here's a -- at least a -- another explanation for the vagueness, I would say, of the document. Would it not have been proper to include that in your report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously I could have included anything, and if Your Honour feels it should have been included, I take your point, and we can use that in the future. As I say, the frame of reference that I was operating in was to use the contemporaneous documentation. We didn't go to other sources of post-conflict information, such as memoirs, press articles, interviews, that type of thing that took place after the end of the conflict. So it was a rather mechanical cutoff from that point of view. But again, if Your Honour feels it is appropriate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course the question was whether you found it appropriate or not, and, of course, this question suggests that at least by the question of appropriateness, so -- to have the question reflected to myself, whether I find it appropriate, is -- I asked you. Of course, the question is about independence, and you'll understand that that's the background of my question. Do the questions raised -- put by the Bench raise any need to further examination, direct examination or any further cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar, I am not quite sure whether we've taken decisions already on all documents tendered into evidence, although they have been numbered. Could you please list them so that we can -- perhaps first of all, we have to deal with the great number of the 19th of December, the instructions documents. I see that we have both B/C/S versions and English translations, and some of them have no translation and some of them have only in English. Would it -- did you give them any sub-numbers, or do you suggest to give them any sub-numbers, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What would the Defence like to do with them? I mean, some -- there was testimony about these documents, so to that extent of course it's not a very substantive issue -- finally, not to be a very substantive matter. But I think it would be better to have them in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And would you consider them to be one bundle or all different? Perhaps we --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We'd say one bundle, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One bundle. But then, of course, we'd have to -- then I suggest the following: That we categorise them by their ERN numbers, that we have a bundle containing and then ERN number so and so, so that there's no confusion about what's in the bundle, especially about whether it's translations, originals, handwritten, cover pages, whatever. I suggest that we do it that way. But then this is not probably the appropriate time to prepare for that and take a final decision, but then perhaps on all the documents at the start next Monday morning, if that would be agreeable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's entirely acceptable, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then is there anything further on the agenda?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, Your Honour, yes, the Prosecution very -- the Prosecution very helpfully overnight had produced for us various printouts of the Cutilheiro Plan. Yes. They gave them to us this morning, since we didn't actually see them in the middle of the night. There are quite a few. They require some sorting out and checking, Your Honour. May we deal with that over the weekend as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I then suggest that you take the best versions of the Cutilheiro Plan which do not -- which are not inconsistent with the ones we saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then if you tender them into evidence. But you should check that we're really talking about from the content the same document as we've seen. Otherwise, of course, you would first have to ask Mr. Treanor whether the Lisbon and the Sarajevo and then perhaps other versions would exist and whether -- what that would mean. Perhaps you could check that with the Prosecution and see whether you agree that we are, from the content, speaking of the same documents and then tender them into evidence. This is not necessarily done right away at 9.00 in the morning next Monday. I further indicate - but that's also in order not to - that the parties will meet for practical matters in this case this afternoon and that the Bench is involved in that communication as well, just in order to avoid whatever impression of secret meetings. Then we adjourn until Monday, the 19th of April in Courtroom II at 9.00, but not Mr. Treanor, after having thanked you for giving your many, many days' evidence, having answered questions of both parties and from the Bench. Very often I have to thank someone also for travelling a long way, but I'll not do that in your case. We are adjourned until next Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 19th day of April, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.50 p.m.,
